say.text: Let's climb the management decisions one rung at a time.
A 45-year-old man has had right iliac fossa pain for five days. Now there is a tender, palpable lump there. He is stable, with a low-grade fever and no peritonitis.
What is your first step?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the omentum and bowel have usually done by day five, and what that means for operating now.
Yes. By day three to five, omentum and loops of bowel have walled the inflamed appendix off as a mass. The Ochsner–Sherren regimen treats it with nil by mouth, IV fluids, IV antibiotics and charting.
Watch for a rising pulse, increasing pain, a growing mass or spreading peritonitis. Any of those means the regimen has failed and surgery is needed.
Tempting: appendicitis means appendicectomy, so operating tonight feels like the decisive move.
But after three to five days the appendix sits inside a walled-off mass. That mass is managed by the Ochsner–Sherren regimen first, and surgery is reserved for the regimen failing.
Which first step fits a walled-off mass?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: appendicitis means surgery is the model to drop once a mass has walled off.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Tempting: a lump in the right iliac fossa sounds like pus, and draining pus feels like the surgical answer.
A mass is not yet an abscess. Open drainage is the fallback when image-guided percutaneous drainage fails, and a mass is treated by the regimen.
Is this patient's lump a mass or a collection of pus?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold this one loosely: a lump is not automatically an abscess, and the regimen comes first for a mass.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Same appendix, a week later. The fever now swings, and imaging shows a collection in the right iliac fossa that can be drained. He is still stable.
What is the best treatment now?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what an abscess needs, and whether the least invasive route can reach it.
Yes. An appendicular abscess is drained, usually percutaneously under image guidance, with antibiotics.
Open drainage is the fallback when this fails, not the first move.
Tempting: fever, pus and a worsening picture make the appendix feel like the thing to remove now.
A drainable collection is treated by drainage with antibiotics first. Emergency appendicectomy is not the first move for an abscess.
What does a drainable abscess need first?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: an abscess that can be drained is drained first.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Tempting: an abscess is pus, and pus is drained, so opening the belly to drain it sounds thorough.
Open drainage is the fallback when image-guided percutaneous drainage fails or is not available. It is not the first step.
Which route does an abscess take first?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold this one loosely: open drainage is the backup, and the image-guided route comes first.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: The lump has settled on the regimen. Now the question is interval surgery.
Which statement about interval appendicectomy is correct in current practice?

choices.label: Routine at 6–8 weeks in every patient
Selective, with colonoscopy or CT in older patients
Never needed once the lump has gone
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check whether the stem asks for the exam key or for current practice, and treat them as two separate statements.
Yes. The PYQ key expects interval appendicectomy at 6–8 weeks. Current practice makes it selective.
Colonoscopy or CT is advised in older patients, over about 40, to exclude caecal carcinoma before deciding.
Tempting: this is the classic answer, and an exam will reward it.
The 6–8 week figure is the exam key. Current practice makes interval surgery selective, not routine for everyone.
What does current practice do before an interval operation in an older patient?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold this one loosely: the classic key and current practice have diverged here.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Tempting: the lump has gone, so the appendix seems to have healed and nothing else needs doing.
Resolution of the mass does not exclude caecal carcinoma. That is why interval surgery is selective, and older patients get colonoscopy or CT.
Is the work-up over once the lump has gone?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a resolved mass is not the end of the question.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Now a patient in whom this matters.
A 55-year-old man's lump has resolved on the regimen. He is well. What is your next step?

choices.label: Colonoscopy or CT first, then selective surgery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask how the patient's age changes the work-up before any interval operation.
Yes. Over about 40, colonoscopy or CT is advised to exclude caecal carcinoma before any interval operation.
Age is the qualifier that drives the work-up here.
Tempting: the PYQ key says interval surgery at 6–8 weeks, and this looks like the textbook sequence.
Age changes the plan. Over about 40 the caecal carcinoma check comes first, so a routine operation with no work-up applies the old key without its qualifier.
What does the work-up look for before the operation?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the 6–8 week key ignores the age qualifier.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Tempting: the regimen worked, but the appendix is still there, so remove it now while he is well.
Immediate surgery is for the regimen failing: rising pulse, growing mass, spreading peritonitis. Here it has worked, so there is no emergency.
Is there an emergency here, or a later decision?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold this one loosely: an operation is triggered by failure of the regimen, not by its success.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Now the operation is not the only option for everyone.
A motivated 40-year-old woman has CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis, with no appendicolith. She asks whether she must have surgery. What is correct?

choices.label: Antibiotics-first is now preferred for all appendicitis
Antibiotics-first is an accepted option for her
Only appendicectomy is ever treatment for her
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which of these is a rule for all patients, and which is a rule for selected ones.
Yes. Antibiotics-first is accepted for selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis.
Tell her that a significant proportion later need appendicectomy for recurrence, so she can weigh that risk before she chooses.
Tempting: appendicectomy is the treatment of choice in every textbook, so 'only treatment' feels like the same statement.
PYQs have expected appendicectomy as the only treatment. Current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected CT-confirmed uncomplicated cases, so the absolute is out of date.
Which statement keeps both ideas: the treatment of choice, and an option for selected patients?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold this one loosely: the old absolute is the exam key, and practice has softened it.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Tempting: antibiotics avoid an operation, so offering them to everyone sounds kinder and more modern.
Antibiotics-first is for selected uncomplicated disease. Complicated disease and an appendicolith do not qualify, and an appendicolith predicts failure.
Which conditions does antibiotics-first depend on?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the qualifiers are what make antibiotics-first an option.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Same kind of scan, one new finding.
A 34-year-old man has CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis. The CT also shows an appendicolith. What is the best management?

choices.label: Antibiotics alone, as the CT shows no perforation
Ochsner–Sherren regimen, as for an appendicular mass
Appendicectomy, as the appendicolith predicts failure
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the appendicolith does to the odds that antibiotics alone will work.
Yes. An appendicolith predicts failure of antibiotics, and faecoliths predominate in adults, where they carry a higher risk of perforation.
Tempting: the CT shows no perforation, so the uncomplicated pathway looks like it applies.
The appendicolith is the qualifier that drops antibiotics-first. It predicts failure and carries a higher risk of perforation.
Which conditions does antibiotics-first depend on?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: no perforation on CT does not remove the appendicolith problem.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Tempting: the inflamed appendix is being treated conservatively, and the regimen looks like a safe default.
The regimen is for an appendicular mass, a walled-off lump. This stem shows no mass, and the regimen is stopped if it fails.
Does this patient have a mass, or uncomplicated appendicitis with an appendicolith?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold this one loosely: the regimen belongs to the mass, not to every inflamed appendix.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: You have chosen the operation. Now the knife.
A 28-year-old had an open appendicectomy through McBurney's point. Weeks later he has a right groin bulge and numbness over the groin. Which nerve was most likely injured?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which nerve lies where the oblique muscles are split near the groin.
Yes. The gridiron is an oblique incision through McBurney's point, and the muscles are split along their fibres.
A groin bulge with groin numbness after this incision points to the ilioinguinal nerve, which can be injured as the muscle is split.
Tempting: iliohypogastric is the neighbouring iliac nerve, and the wound sits close to it.
Injury to the ilioinguinal nerve with a gridiron incision is the one that gives a right inguinal hernia. The gridiron splits the muscles this nerve runs through.
Which nerve runs through the muscle split and gives the groin bulge?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the neighbour nerve is not the one the incision threatens.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Tempting: a groin symptom feels like a genitofemoral problem, since that nerve lies near the inguinal region.
The hernia after a gridiron comes from the ilioinguinal nerve, not the genitofemoral. Name the nerve by the incision you used.
Which nerve does the gridiron put at risk?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold this one loosely: pair the incision with its nerve, not with a neighbour.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Now the complications, and one split that matters: does it come from the disease or from the knife?
Which is the most common complication after appendicectomy?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether the complication comes from the disease or from the knife.
Yes. Wound infection is the most common complication of the operation itself.
It sits on the knife side. Abscess and pylephlebitis sit on the disease side.
Tempting: pylephlebitis is a serious infection that follows appendicitis, so it feels like a post-op problem.
Pylephlebitis is septic thrombophlebitis of the portal veins, with jaundice and liver abscesses. It comes from the disease, not from the wound or the stump.
Does it come from the disease, or from the knife?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a complication that spreads through the portal system is a disease complication.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: Tempting: an abscess after surgery feels like a post-op complication.
An appendicular abscess is a disease complication: a collection that forms from the inflamed appendix, listed with the mass.
Which list does the most common post-op complication belong to?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold this one loosely: an abscess here is a complication of the disease.

choices.label: Move on, I'll come back to it

say.text: The idea of this ladder: decide by stage, by patient group, and by whether a complication comes from the disease or from the knife. A mass is treated conservatively; an abscess is drained; uncomplicated disease can take antibiotics-first in selected adults, but not with an appendicolith; older patients get colonoscopy or CT before interval surgery.
After surgery, wound infection is the commonest complication, and the nerve to name at the gridiron is the ilioinguinal.
